RagShortTexts: Granada survived as the final Muslim oasis through tribute to Castile, fortifying the Alhambra.

Variants.Content: Sheltered beneath the Sierra Nevada, the Emirate of Granada emerged under Muhammad I ibn Nasr as the last surviving Islamic realm in Iberia. The Nasrid dynasty rose after Almohad power collapsed in al-Andalus, and its survival depended on two things: substantial gold parias paid to the Crown of Castile in exchange for autonomy, and the red citadel of the Alhambra, fortified on the hill above the city. The emirate's irrigated valleys produced silk and fruit, and its craftsmen, scholars, and merchants kept Andalusian culture alive for centuries. Granada was a small realm wedged between a powerful Christian kingdom and the sea, and its rulers survived by knowing when to pay and when to hold their ground.

The Nasrid emirs ruled through diplomatic finesse and gold that came north along the Saharan trade. By humouring Castilian kings with tributary allegiance, they kept Christian armies at bay, while open ports to the Marinid sultans of Fez gave them a second ally. A chamberlain who misread the mood at Toledo or Fez could see the treasury drained or the Alhambra besieged.

Nasrid jinetes ride light horses of Arabian bloodline, and they loose javelins at a full gallop through the mountain passes. A man who grew up in the serranía knows every goat track and can vanish into the rocks after one volley. Heavy northern knights who climb into the high country find their armour a deadly burden in narrow defiles.
Refugees from Seville and Cordoba engineered terraced aqueducts fed by snowmelt. Heavy tributes weigh upon our looms, but silk mills hum and the call to prayer rings true across the green Vega.
